noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: identify the chemical elements present in carbohydrates, proteins and lipids (fats and oils)

describe the structure of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids as large molecules made up from smaller basic units: starch and glycogen from simple sugars, protein from amino acids, and lipid from fatty acids and glycerol

primer.text: Three families of large molecules run almost every job in a living organism: carbohydrates, lipids and proteins. This note fixes what each family is made of — their chemical elements and their smaller building units — because exam questions love asking you to connect a molecule to its elements and to the units it is assembled from.

lessons.title: Elements first, then the carbohydrate family
lessons.opening: Every molecule in the three biological families contains carbon, which is why they are called organic. Carbohydrates carry carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in various sizes: single simple sugars, pairs joined together, or long chains built from many glucose units. Starch and glycogen matter most, because they are the storage forms plants and animals rely on.
keyPoints: Carbohydrates, proteins and lipids all contain carbon, which makes them organic molecules.
A simple sugar such as glucose is the single-unit member of the carbohydrate family.
Two joined simple sugars make maltose; long chains of many glucose units build starch, glycogen and cellulose.
Polysaccharides suit storage because their large insoluble molecules stay put inside cells.

low.restatement: All three families contain carbon. Carbohydrates run from single sugars like glucose up to long chains — starch and glycogen store energy, cellulose builds walls.
low.analogy: Simple sugars are Lego bricks: one brick, a pair snapped together, or a full wall of bricks locked end to end.
low.examPointer: The elements test is a gift if you learn it as a table row: carbohydrate CHO, protein CHON, lipid CHO.

medium.restatement: Chain length is the organising principle of the carbohydrate family: solubility falls as chains grow, which is exactly why the longest members serve as storage or structural material.
medium.analogy: A single sugar is a loose coin that slips away easily; a polysaccharide is a rolled, wrapped bundle that stays in your pocket.
medium.examPointer: Link the insolubility of starch and glycogen to their storage role in a 'why' question — the causal chain earns the second mark.

check.stem: Which chemical elements do carbohydrates contain?

options.explanation: The note lists exactly these three elements.
Nitrogen belongs to proteins, not carbohydrates.
The nitrogen addition describes proteins.
Oxygen is always present too.

check.stem: What joins together to build starch and glycogen?

options.explanation: Cellulose is itself a glucose polymer, not a building block.

options.text: Many glucose molecules linked in long chains
options.explanation: Both polymers are built from many glucose units.
Those build lipids.
Those build proteins.

check.stem: Why are polysaccharides useful as storage molecules?

options.text: Because they carry nitrogen for growth
options.explanation: Carbohydrates carry no nitrogen.

options.text: Because they are the smallest sugars available
options.explanation: They are the largest members of the family.

options.text: Because they are large and insoluble, so they stay in place inside cells
options.explanation: The note links insolubility to the storage role.

options.text: Because they dissolve quickly into the blood
options.explanation: Insolubility, not solubility, suits storage.

check.stem: Maltose is formed when which two units join?

options.explanation: Fatty acids build lipids.
That would build a protein fragment.
Glycerol belongs to lipids.
The note names maltose as two glucose molecules joined.

check.stem: A molecule list reads: glucose, maltose, starch, cellulose. Which family do all four belong to, and what changes along the list?

options.text: Carbohydrates; the molecules grow from single units to very long chains
options.explanation: All four are carbohydrates and the list runs by increasing chain length.

options.text: Lipids; they grow from oils to fats
options.explanation: None of the four is a lipid.

options.text: Proteins; they grow by adding amino acids
options.explanation: None of the four is a protein.

options.text: A mixed list with no single family
options.explanation: All four sit in one family.

check.stem: State the three chemical elements carbohydrates contain.
Name the polysaccharide that plants use for storage and the one animals use.
check.modelAnswer: Plants store starch; animals store glycogen.

check.stem: Explain why cellulose, starch and glycogen can all be built from the same single unit yet play different roles.
check.modelAnswer: All three are long chains of glucose units, but chain length, the way chains branch and where they are placed differ, so the same building block yields a wall material in plants, a plant energy store and an animal energy store.

check.stem: An athlete's trainer suggests a slow-release carbohydrate meal before a long race. Using chain length, explain which family member fits that description.
check.modelAnswer: A long-chain polysaccharide such as starch fits: its large insoluble molecules must be broken down step by step into glucose, releasing energy steadily rather than in one jump the way a drink of simple sugar would.

lessons.title: Lipids and proteins: units, shapes and jobs
lessons.opening: Lipids — fats and oils — are assembled from glycerol joined to fatty acids, and their state at room temperature decides the everyday name. Proteins are built from amino acids joined in any order, which is why hundreds of thousands of different proteins exist. Each protein's sequence gives it a specific shape, and the shape decides the job.
keyPoints: Lipids are large molecules built from glycerol and fatty acids joined together.
Solid lipids at room temperature are called fats and liquid ones are called oils.
Proteins are built from amino acids joined in sequences that vary enormously.
A protein's amino acid sequence fixes its overall shape, and the shape determines its function.

low.restatement: Lipids = glycerol + fatty acids; fats are solid, oils liquid. Proteins = amino acid chains; the order of the units shapes the molecule and its job.
low.analogy: Lipids come as one hub with a few spokes (glycerol with fatty acids); proteins are bead necklaces where bead order changes the necklace completely.
low.examPointer: Learn both unit pairs verbatim: glycerol with fatty acids for lipids, amino acids for proteins — 'smaller units' questions are near-guaranteed marks.

medium.restatement: The protein shape-function link is the deep idea: sequence dictates shape, shape dictates binding, and changing the sequence can destroy the binding site that makes the protein useful.
medium.analogy: A protein works like a key cut from its bead order — recut the beads and the key no longer fits its lock.
medium.examPointer: Name enzymes, haemoglobin and keratin as protein examples; linking each to its job shows the shape-function principle in action.

check.stem: Which pair of smaller units builds lipids?

options.explanation: The note names exactly this pair.
Those are carbohydrate units.
Those build proteins.
Nucleotides build nucleic acids, outside this note.

check.stem: Which statement about lipid behaviour at room temperature is correct?

options.explanation: Both store energy richly.

options.text: They are both lipids, differing in their state at room temperature
options.explanation: Solid lipids are fats and liquid lipids are oils.

options.text: Fats are carbohydrates and oils are lipids
options.explanation: Both belong to the lipid family.

options.text: Oils contain nitrogen while fats do not
options.explanation: Neither contains nitrogen.

check.stem: Why can organisms build hundreds of thousands of different proteins?

options.text: Because every protein uses exactly the same order
options.explanation: A fixed order would give one protein.

options.text: Because proteins link to carbohydrates in varied ways
options.explanation: The family builds from amino acids alone.

options.text: Because amino acids can be arranged in many different orders
options.explanation: Sequence variety is the stated source of protein diversity.

options.text: Because amino acids can turn into glycerol
options.explanation: Amino acids do not become lipid units.

check.stem: What decides a protein's overall shape?

options.explanation: Temperature affects shape but does not determine the designed shape.

options.text: The amount of starch stored nearby
options.explanation: Carbohydrate stores are unrelated to protein shape.

options.text: The number of fatty acids attached
options.explanation: Fatty acids belong to lipids.
Sequence gives the molecule its particular shape.

check.stem: Which list contains only proteins named in this note?

options.explanation: All three are named protein examples.
Starch is a carbohydrate.
Glycogen is a carbohydrate.
Triglyceride is a lipid.

check.stem: Name the smaller units proteins are built from.
Give the two smaller units lipids are built from.
Explain why a change in a protein's amino acid sequence can stop the protein doing its job.
check.modelAnswer: The sequence determines the overall shape of the molecule, and the shape determines what the protein can bind or catalyse; altering the sequence can reshape the working region so it no longer fits its target, leaving the protein unable to function.

check.stem: A seed contains an energy store and a structural material for new membranes. Which two molecule families and unit pairs should the seed be rich in?
check.modelAnswer: The energy store should be a lipid (built from glycerol and fatty acids) and the membrane material also draws on lipids, while any growth machinery will need proteins built from amino acids — so the seed banks both families.

glossary.definition: A large carbohydrate built from many simple sugar units joined in a chain.
The backbone unit that joins fatty acids to build lipids.
The repeating unit that joins in varying orders to build proteins.
Describes molecules that contain carbon, including all three biological families here.
